a1-pronouns-copula.title: Pronouns & the Verb "To Be"
a1-pronouns-copula.pattern: ӕз дӕн (I am) · ды дӕ (you are) · уый у (he/she/it is) · мах стӕм (we are) · сымах стут (you all are) · уыдон сты (they are)
a1-pronouns-copula.explanation: Unlike its Northeast Caucasian neighbors (Chechen, Avar), where "to be" changes shape to agree with the grammatical class of its SUBJECT NOUN, Ossetian's copula conjugates by PERSON, much like Russian or English "to be": ӕз (I) takes дӕн, ды (you) takes дӕ, уый (he/she/it) takes у, мах (we) takes стӕм, сымах (you-plural) takes стут, and уыдон (they) takes сты.
a1-pronouns-copula.fact: The 3rd-person singular has a second, less common form, ис, alongside у -- academic sources treat these as having a subtle distinction (existential vs. predicative), which is genuinely nuanced enough that this course only teaches у for now rather than risk blurring the two together incorrectly.

a2-possession.title: Possession: мӕ (my) & дӕ (your)
a2-possession.explanation: мӕ and дӕ go directly before the noun they possess, with no other change to the noun itself: мӕ телефон (my phone), дӕ къухтӕ (your hands). дӕ is the same word you already know as the "you are" copula (дӕ) -- Ossetian genuinely reuses this one small word for both jobs, and context tells them apart.
a2-possession.fact: "Мӕ телефон дзуры!" ("My phone is ringing!") uses дзуры, the same verb that usually means "speaks" -- Ossetian extends "speak" to cover a ringing phone, much like some English speakers might say a phone is "talking" to them.

a2-origin.title: Origin: -ӕй (from a place)
a2-origin.explanation: To say where someone is from, Ossetian adds -ӕй directly onto the place name and follows it with the copula: Аргентинӕйӕ дӕн (I'm from Argentina), Берлинӕй дӕ? (are you from Berlin?). This course only uses -ӕй with these two specific place names, both independently confirmed -- the suffix likely generalizes to other places too, but that hasn't been confirmed here yet.
a2-origin.fact: The two confirmed examples (Argentina, Berlin) are both foreign place names borrowed into Ossetian largely as-is, with just -ӕй added -- a good sign that this suffix attaches easily to loanwords, though the details for native Ossetian place names aren't confirmed yet.

a2-past-copula.title: Past Tense: To Be (partial)
a2-past-copula.pattern: уыдтӕн (I was) · уыди (he/she/it was) · уыдысты (they were)
a2-past-copula.explanation: "To be" has its own past-tense forms, built on a different stem (уыд-) from the present (у/ис): Ахуыргӕнӕг уыдтӕн (I was a teacher), Фын уыди (it was a dream), Сӕхимӕ уыдысты? (were they at home?).
a2-past-copula.fact: Only three persons of this past-tense paradigm are confirmed so far (I/he-she-it/they) -- the "you" and "we" forms aren't taught yet since a clean confirmed example hasn't turned up.

a2-verbs-more.title: More Verbs in Full Conjugation
a2-verbs-more.pattern: хъусын (to hear) · уынын (to see), conjugated across persons
a2-verbs-more.explanation: More practice with the full present-tense pattern you already know, applied to two more verbs: хъусын (to hear) -> хъусын/хъусыс/хъусы/хъусӕм/хъусут/хъусынц, and уынын (to see) -> уынын/уынис/уыны/уынӕм/уынут/уынынц.
a2-verbs-more.fact: уынын is a great example of the 1sg-equals-infinitive rule in action: on its own it's ambiguous between "to see" and "I see", and only the sentence around it (or a subject pronoun) tells you which.

a2-verbs-more-2.title: Even More Verbs Conjugated
a2-verbs-more-2.pattern: фидын (to pay) · хонын (to call), conjugated across persons
a2-verbs-more-2.explanation: More practice with the same confirmed present-tense pattern, applied to two more verbs: фидын (to pay) -> фидын/фиды/фидӕм, and хонын (to call) -> хонын/хоны/хонӕм.
a2-verbs-more-2.fact: By now you've seen this exact -ын/-ыс/-ы/-ӕм/-ут/-ынц pattern applied to nine different verbs across this course -- it's one of the most reliable, reusable patterns in the whole language.

a2-present-full.title: Present Tense: Full Conjugation
a2-present-full.explanation: Now that you know the "you"-form (-ыс), here's the complete present-tense pattern for regular verbs, using дзурын ("to speak") as the model: дзурын (I speak -- identical in form to the infinitive itself), дзурыс (you speak), дзуры (he/she/it speaks), дзурӕм (we speak), дзурут (you all speak), дзурынц (they speak).
a2-present-full.fact: The 1st-person-singular present is spelled exactly like the infinitive (дзурын means both "to speak" and "I speak") -- context and the subject pronoun are what tell them apart, not the verb form itself. Every one of these six endings is independently attested in natural sentences, not derived by a single blanket rule.

a2-present-2sg-negation.title: Present Tense (You): -ыс & Negation: нӕй
a2-present-2sg-negation.explanation: Regular verbs form the "you" (singular) present tense by dropping the infinitive ending -ын and adding -ыс: дзурын (to speak) -> дзурыс (you speak), хӕрын (to eat) -> хӕрыс (you eat). To negate the copula in the present tense, Ossetian uses the special fused form нӕй ("is not") rather than combining нӕ with у.
a2-present-2sg-negation.fact: нӕй isn't simply нӕ ("not") plus у glued together -- it's its own fused negative form, which is why it looks different from what you might expect. This course only teaches the "you"-form of regular verbs and the 3rd-person negative copula for now; the rest of the person/tense paradigm needs more confirmation before being taught.

b1-conv-possession.title: Conversation: Do You Have It?
b1-conv-possession.explanation: "Мӕнмӕ ис X" (lit. "to-me is X") is a common way Ossetian expresses "I have X" -- built from attested sentences here, not asserted as a full productive rule, since the exact case-marking system behind it isn't independently confirmed yet.
b1-conv-possession.fact: This "to-me is X" possession pattern is shared by many languages across the Caucasus region, not unique to Ossetian.

b1-conv-everyday.title: Conversation: Checking In
b1-conv-everyday.explanation: "Куыддӕ?" (how are you?) is one of the most common things you'll actually hear in conversation. These lines are attested, real sentences from native speakers -- sequenced here as a natural back-and-forth, not asserted as a fixed script.
b1-conv-everyday.fact: Ossetian yes/no questions are often made just by tone/context (Кусы. "It works." vs Кусы? "Is it working?") rather than a special question word -- the same word can be a statement or a question depending on how it's said.

b1-conv-invite.title: Conversation: Making Plans
b1-conv-invite.explanation: Real invitations and small plans, built from attested sentences: suggesting to go somewhere, asking when, and agreeing.
b1-conv-invite.fact: "Цом!" is an everyday, casual way to say "Let's go!/Come on!" -- much more common in speech than a longer grammatical construction would be.

b1-hquama-phrases.title: Fixed Phrase: хъуама (must/should)
b1-hquama-phrases.explanation: хъуама means "must/should", but the verb that follows it takes a special subjunctive-like form that isn't a simple rule yet confirmed from a reliable source. Rather than guess at how to build new sentences with it, this course presents the two attested examples as fixed phrases to recognize.
b1-hquama-phrases.fact: Both attested examples use different-looking verb endings (акӕной, фӕхонай) even though both mean roughly "must do something" -- a sign that the rule behind them is more complex than "хъуама + one fixed ending", which is exactly why it's not taught as a productive pattern yet.

b1-need-want.title: Need/Want: мӕ ... хъӕуы
b1-need-want.explanation: To say you need or want something, Ossetian puts the experiencer (мӕ, "to me") before the thing needed, and хъӕуы ("is needed/wanted") after it: Дон мӕ хъӕуы literally means "water to-me is-needed", i.e. "I'm thirsty" / "I need water". This is the same pattern you've already seen with possession (мӕ телефон, "my phone") and negation (нӕй) -- Ossetian keeps reusing a small set of building blocks in new combinations.
b1-need-want.fact: The corpus this course draws from also shows a second, different-looking construction (an allative suffix -мӕ attached directly to the noun, as in "Скутермӕ хъӕуы" for "I want a scooter") -- that's a materially different pattern from this one and isn't taught yet, to avoid mixing up two constructions that look similar but work differently.
